summary: This article compares special education and inclusive education policies across countries, looking at how teacher training, resourcing, evaluation, technology, cultural attitudes and international partnerships shape outcomes for students with disabilities. It contrasts Scandinavia's universal design approach with the fragmented US system under IDEA and cites developments in Finland, Australia, Canada, Germany, Korea, Japan, Latin America and Africa. It concludes that the best policies are flexible, well-resourced and paired with shifts in societal attitudes.
one_line: A comparative look at how countries' special and inclusive education policies, training, funding, technology and culture affect students with disabilities.
key_facts: On September 3, 2023, the United Nations re-emphasized inclusive education under Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education), prompting nations to revisit their policies.

Dr. Ellen Copeland, an educational psychologist, says inclusion is not merely about physical spaces in mainstream schools but also tailored teaching methods, curriculum adaptations and supportive environments.
Scandinavian countries have long adopted principles of universal design in learning, so educational environments are inherently accessible to all students.
The United States governs special education mainly through the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), in place since the mid-1970s, but practices vary greatly from state to state.
Professor John Miller of the University of California describes US inclusion as 'a patchwork of policies'.
In Finland, teachers receive specialized training for diverse student needs; teacher Aino Korhonen says 'Every teacher is effectively a special education teacher to some extent.'
On October 15, 2023, Australia launched the 'Inclusive Teacher Programme' to introduce comprehensive training modules for inclusive education.
A UNESCO 2024 report found that in some parts of Africa only 2% of teachers have received adequate training to support students with special needs.
On November 12, 2023, Canada's government announced a significant funding increase for special education resources, including assistive technologies and support personnel.
In Germany, educator Hans Schulz notes disparities in resource distribution between rural and urban areas that affect students with special needs.
The Republic of Korea has pioneered an evaluation system tracking inclusion programs by student well-being and academic achievement.
Japan's Ministry of Education introduced an e-learning platform tailored for students with disabilities in January 2024.
In Latin America, stigma and discrimination remain barriers to inclusive education; Brazilian reformer Paulo Silva says mindsets must change first.
The International Alliance for Inclusive Education was formed on February 8, 2024, to foster cross-border collaboration on inclusive policies.
